title: Hooked: How to Build Habit-Forming Products
note: DB Turkish title 'Müşteriyi Anlamak' is not a faithful title. Facts verified in the full text of Hooked (archive.org djvu text, 'with Ryan Hoover').

facts.claim: The Hook Model has four phases: trigger, action, variable reward and investment.

Yin (not her real name) is in her mid-twenties, lives in Palo Alto, attends Stanford and is compulsively hooked on Instagram; she snaps and posts dozens of pictures a day, moody snapshots filtered to look like the late 1970s.
Instagram was purchased by Facebook for $1 billion in 2012 and had 150 million users (at the time of writing); Eyal notes the price was driven by many factors including a rumored bidding war.
Yin quote: 'It's just fun. I don't have a problem or anything. I just use it whenever I see something cool. I feel I need to grab it before it's gone.'

Yin's habit started with an external trigger, a friend's recommendation, and weeks of repeated use. Her photos shared on Facebook and Twitter act as external triggers for others; others found the app via media, bloggers and Apple's App Store featuring; once installed, the app icon and push notifications call users back.

With repeated use the cue moves inside: the fear of losing a special moment brings a pang of stress, and the user opens Instagram to capture a photo. Instagram also relieves boredom and fear of missing out.

Habits are like pearls: an irritant inside the oyster triggers layers of nacre; triggers are the grit new habits build on. New habits are sparked by external triggers, but associations with internal triggers keep users hooked; this can take weeks or months.
Negative emotions (boredom, loneliness, frustration, confusion, indecisiveness) are powerful internal triggers that prompt an almost instant, often mindless action to quell the feeling.

Missouri University of Science and Technology: in 2011, 216 undergraduates volunteered to have their internet activity tracked anonymously over the academic year; researchers compared the data of students treated at university health services for depression symptoms. Sriram Chellappan: participants with depressive symptoms 'tended to engage in very high email usage', plus more video watching, gaming and chatting. Eyal: the study showed people with depression symptoms used the internet more; one hypothesis is that they seek relief from negative emotions.
Eyal's examples: bored people turn to dramatic headlines, stressed people to Pinterest, lonely people to Facebook and Twitter, uncertainty to Google; email checks whether someone needs us.

In the 1950s B.F. Skinner put pigeons in a box that delivered a food pellet each time they pressed a lever; then the machine released food after a random number of taps. The intermittent reward dramatically increased how often the pigeons tapped.

Eyal proposes three types of variable reward: tribe (social), hunt (resources, information), self (mastery, completion). Email uses all three: who wrote (tribe), what opportunity or threat it brings (hunt), the urge to clear unread messages and control the inbox (self).
Twitter's feed mixes mundane and relevant content; sometimes a user finds interesting news, sometimes not, and keeps scrolling. Slot machines are a classic reward of the hunt.

rejected.claim: 'Uncertain reward is always more addictive than certain reward.'
rejected.reason: Overgeneralization not stated in the book.
